title: Cross-Dataset Generalization of Jailbreaks: Do Attacks Tuned on StrongReject Transfer to AILuminate?

evidence: JailbreakBench (NeurIPS 2024) provides an open robustness benchmark standardizing jailbreak evaluation across models, but does not specifically compare StrongReject vs AILuminate attack rankings.
AILuminate v0.5 (MLCommons, Dec 2025) measures adversarial resilience with public jailbreak attacks, but no published study directly compares attack rank-order across StrongReject and AILuminate.
JailBreakV-28K (COLM 2024) studies transferability of jailbreak techniques across modalities, establishing methodology for cross-benchmark transfer studies.
The specific question of whether top attacks on StrongReject rank differently on AILuminate has not been directly studied, though the methodology and benchmarks exist.

title: Decoding Parameter Attacks on 4-bit Quantized Models: Does Quantization Alter Attack Surface?

evidence: Qi et al. (2024) 'Fine-tuning Aligned Language Models Compromises Safety' shows quantization has variable effects on jailbreak success rates.
Alignment-Aware Quantization (AAQ, Nov 2025, arXiv:2511.07842) proposes alignment-preserving 4-bit W4A4 quantization, directly addressing the quantization-safety tradeoff.
ResearchGate (2025) 'Quantization-based Jailbreaking Vulnerability Analysis' studies Llama3-8B-Instruct under quantization, closely overlapping with this idea.
Generation exploitation attacks (Huang et al., Princeton) show decoding parameter manipulation increases misalignment 0% to 95%, but this was done on full-precision models.

The specific combination of decoding parameter attacks (temperature, top-p sweeps) on GPTQ/AWQ 4-bit variants has partial overlap with existing work but the exact experimental design is not fully replicated.

title: Replicating the Simple Adaptive Attack (ICLR 2025) on Llama-3.1-8B with Varying Iteration Budgets

evidence: The Simple Adaptive Attack paper (ICLR 2025, arXiv:2404.02151) already reports 100% ASR on Llama-3-Instruct-8B using random search suffix optimization with logprob maximization.
The paper's GitHub repo (tml-epfl/llm-adaptive-attacks) provides full code for reproducing attacks with configurable iteration budgets.
The paper already demonstrates attack effectiveness across multiple models and discusses query efficiency, which directly relates to iteration budget analysis.
Extending to Llama-3.1-8B specifically is a minor variant; the attack methodology and iteration-budget sensitivity are already characterized in the original work.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Reduced from 4: the original paper already demonstrates the attack works on Llama-3 variants with 100% ASR. Replicating on Llama-3.1-8B with iteration budgets provides incremental rather than novel safety landscape information.

title: Free Jailbreak Detection Across Tokenizer Families: Does Tokenizer Choice Affect First-Token Confidence Signals?

evidence: The FJD paper (EMNLP 2025 Findings, arXiv:2509.14558) introduces first-token confidence as a jailbreak detection signal and demonstrates its effectiveness, but evaluates on a limited set of models.
The FJD paper does not systematically investigate how different tokenizer architectures (BPE variants across Llama, Mistral, Gemma families) affect detection reliability.
No follow-up work was found that specifically tests FJD's cross-tokenizer robustness or identifies tokenizer-dependent failure modes.
The question of whether tokenizer vocabulary differences cause systematic AUROC degradation for FJD is an open and practical research question.

title: Shallow Alignment After Domain Fine-Tuning: Does Medical QA Fine-Tuning Deepen or Erode First-Token Safety?

evidence: Qi et al. (ICLR 2025) 'Safety Alignment Should Be Made More Than Just a Few Tokens Deep' establishes shallow alignment as concentrated in first few tokens and shows fine-tuning erodes it.
Re-Emergent Misalignment (arXiv:2507.03662) demonstrates that narrow domain fine-tuning causes broad, domain-agnostic safety erosion.
Multiple papers (2024-2025) confirm fine-tuning even on benign data degrades safety alignment.

The specific angle of measuring first-token concentration changes after medical QA fine-tuning is a specific instantiation of well-characterized phenomena, though the medical domain focus and token-level spatial analysis adds some specificity.

title: Crescendo Multi-Turn Jailbreaks Under Varying System Prompt Lengths: Does Richer Context Help?

evidence: The Crescendo paper (USENIX Security 2025) demonstrates the multi-turn jailbreak attack but does not systematically study defense via system prompt enrichment.
Research shows Crescendo resists conventional detection since it uses benign-looking prompts, but no study varies system prompt length/detail as a defense variable.
Follow-up work on multi-turn defenses (Jan 2026) focuses on internal activation monitoring rather than system prompt engineering.
The specific hypothesis that richer system prompts could reduce Crescendo ASR is untested in the literature. Both positive and negative results would be informative.

title: Cross-Modality Adversarial Suffix Transfer: Do Text-Optimized GCG Suffixes Boost ASR on Code Prompts?

evidence: GCG suffix transferability has been studied across models (Zou et al., 2023) but not specifically across prompt modalities (natural language vs code).
CodeLlama-specific jailbreak evaluation is sparse in the literature; most jailbreak studies focus on general-purpose chat models.
Adversarial Prompt Translation (2024) improves GCG transfer across models but does not address text-to-code domain transfer.
The specific question of whether code-structured prompts interact differently with text-optimized adversarial suffixes appears unstudied.

title: Shallow Alignment in Reasoning Models: Does Chain-of-Thought Change First-Token Safety Concentration?

evidence: Qi et al. (ICLR 2025) establishes the shallow alignment framework showing safety concentrates in first few tokens, but does not study reasoning models specifically.

SafeThinker (arXiv:2601.16506, Jan 2026) explicitly addresses shallow alignment in reasoning models, proposing an adaptive framework with a gateway classifier to deepen safety beyond first tokens in CoT models.
Trend Micro (Mar 2025) published research on exploiting DeepSeek-R1 CoT security, demonstrating that the CoT structure creates exploitable attack surfaces.
SafePath (2025) proposes early alignment intervention during reasoning and is 295x faster than direct refusal for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B.

The specific measurement of refusal location distribution (CoT vs answer section) and prefilling the answer section is partially addressed by SafeThinker and related work, though the precise experimental design differs.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Maintained at 4: while SafeThinker and SafePath address related questions, the specific empirical measurement of refusal-prefix concentration in CoT vs answer sections and targeted answer-section prefilling attacks remains a valuable contribution.

title: Jailbreak Benchmark Agreement Study: Do StrongReject and TrustLLM Rank Models Consistently?

evidence: The StrongREJECT paper (Souly et al., 2024) explicitly compares its evaluator against others and notes TrustLLM only evaluates static templates while StrongREJECT provides more nuanced scoring.
JailbreakBench (NeurIPS 2024) provides standardized evaluation but acknowledges benchmark fragmentation as an open problem.
Sorry-Bench (ICLR 2025) studies evaluation methodology for jailbreaks, addressing evaluator agreement but not full benchmark-to-benchmark model ranking comparison.
A direct Spearman correlation study of model rankings between StrongReject and TrustLLM has not been published, but the methodological differences are already documented.

title: Indirect Prompt Injection via RAG Documents Exploits Shallow Alignment: A Direct vs. Indirect Comparison

evidence: Indirect prompt injection in RAG systems is extensively studied (OWASP LLM01:2025), with poison-RAG attacks achieving >90% ASR.
Shallow alignment vulnerability is well-characterized (Qi et al., ICLR 2025) showing safety concentrates in first tokens.
Adaptive attacks break defenses against indirect prompt injection (NAACL 2025 Findings).

The specific angle of connecting shallow alignment theory to RAG injection by measuring refusal-prefix concentration across direct vs indirect pathways adds theoretical depth, but the core finding that RAG injection bypasses safety is well-established.
Narrow Fine-Tuning Erodes Safety Alignment in Vision-Language Agents (Feb 2026) extends the alignment erosion concept to agents, which includes RAG-like retrieval.

title: Training Activation Probes Without Labeled Harmful Examples: Contrastive Pairs as a Substitute

evidence: Representational Contrastive Scoring (RCS, Dec 2025, arXiv:2512.12069) uses contrastive detection methods (MCD, KCD) in internal representations to separate benign and malicious inputs, achieving SOTA on unseen attack types.
JBShield (USENIX Security 2025) uses Linear Representation Hypothesis to define toxic and jailbreak concepts in activation space without requiring extensive labeled harmful examples.
A learnable anomaly detection framework (2025) optimizes safety-related extraction from internal activations in an unsupervised manner.
Hiding in Plain Text (Feb 2026, arXiv:2602.19396) introduces activation disentanglement with a contrastive goal-framing corpus for jailbreak detection.

The specific proposal of using contrastive pairs (benign vs harmful reformulations) to train probes without labeled harmful outputs overlaps substantially with RCS and related work, though the exact contrastive pair construction may differ.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Reduced from 4: multiple recent papers (RCS, JBShield, unsupervised anomaly detection) already demonstrate activation-based jailbreak detection without extensive labeled harmful data. The gap this idea aims to fill has been partially closed.

title: Token Budget Enforcement as a Cheap Defense: Does Forcing Short Responses Reduce Jailbreak Utility?

evidence: No published study was found that systematically evaluates max_tokens enforcement as a jailbreak defense mechanism.
Token limit research focuses on context window management and input truncation rather than output truncation as a safety measure.
The BOOST attack (2025) exploits eos tokens for jailbreaking, showing token-level manipulation is a live research area, but from the attack side rather than defense.
Talk Too Much (2024) studies poisoning under token limits but from an attack perspective, not evaluating truncation as defense.
The simple hypothesis that truncated harmful outputs may have reduced utility is intuitive but untested empirically.

title: Greedy vs. Sampling Decoding and First-Token Safety Concentration: Is Low Temperature Already a Partial Bypass?

evidence: Huang et al. (Princeton, 2024) 'Catastrophic Jailbreak of Open-source LLMs via Exploiting Generation' demonstrates generation exploitation attacks increasing misalignment 0% to 95% across 11 LLMs by manipulating temperature, top-p, and top-k.

Qi et al. (ICLR 2025) 'Safety Alignment Should Be Made More Than Just a Few Tokens Deep' explicitly identifies decoding parameter exploits as a consequence of shallow alignment and discusses how random sampling deviates from refusal tokens.
The FJD paper (EMNLP 2025) uses temperature scaling on logits as part of its detection method, directly connecting temperature to first-token safety signals.
The specific combination of temperature variation + first-token concentration measurement is well-covered between the shallow alignment paper and the generation exploitation paper.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Reduced from 4: the generation exploitation paper already demonstrates that temperature manipulation catastrophically breaks safety alignment across 11 models, and the shallow alignment paper explicitly identifies this as a known vulnerability. The core finding is already established.

elimination_reason: Novelty score 2 (largely_addressed). The core research question -- whether sampling temperature bypasses shallow safety alignment -- is directly answered by Huang et al. (2024) demonstrating 0% to 95% misalignment via decoding parameter manipulation, and Qi et al. (ICLR 2025) explicitly identifying decoding parameter attacks as a consequence of shallow alignment. Both the attack mechanism and first-token concentration connection are published.

title: Cross-Attack Generalization of Activation Probes: Does Training on Suffix Attacks Detect Role-Play Jailbreaks?

evidence: JBShield (USENIX Security 2025) uses concept-based analysis to detect jailbreaks and evaluates cross-attack detection by separating toxic concepts from jailbreak concepts.
RCS (Dec 2025) achieves SOTA on evaluation protocols designed to test generalization to unseen attack types using contrastive methods in internal representations.
The ICLR 2025 paper on jailbreak features investigates what prompt features enable jailbreaks, providing mechanistic understanding relevant to cross-attack generalization.

The specific experimental setup of training probes on suffix attacks and testing on role-play jailbreaks is a natural ablation that is partially covered by JBShield's cross-attack evaluation, though not with this exact train/test split.

title: GCG Text Suffix Attacks on Vision-Language Models: Does the Image Modality Affect Optimization Efficiency?

evidence: Bi-Modal Adversarial Prompt (BAP, 2025) attacks combine visual overlays and textual cues for VLM jailbreaks, studying the interaction between modalities.
Universal and Transferable Jailbreak Attacks on VLMs (Feb 2026, arXiv:2602.01025) directly addresses VLM-specific jailbreak methodology.
GCG-based image attacks adapt the GCG loss to optimize adversarial images instead of text suffixes, showing the image modality is already being studied as an alternative attack surface.

The specific question of whether a benign image's presence changes text-space GCG optimization efficiency is a narrow variant not directly answered, but the broader VLM jailbreak landscape is active and partially overlapping.
